Assigned to Futuna, he landed in November 1837, the first Christian missionary ever to set foot there. Amid great hardship he learned the language, treated the sick, and began to win converts. King Niuliki, jealous of the new faith and angered by his children's conversion, had Chanel assassinated on 28 April 1841. Within a year the whole island turned Christian, fulfilling his hope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-raphael-th:
Raphael, whose name means God has healed, appears in Scripture only in the Book of Tobit. He is absent from the Hebrew Scriptures and enters the Septuagint as the travelling companion of young Tobias, calling himself Azarias son of the great Ananias. The journey in Tobit 5 to 11 shows his protective care at every turn.

He binds in the desert of Upper Egypt the demon who had slain seven husbands of Sara, daughter of Raguel, and after the return he heals the blindness of elder Tobias. Then he reveals himself as the angel Raphael, one of the seven who stand before the Lord. With Gabriel and Michael he forms the trio named in canonical Scripture. The entry surveys his place in angelology, art, and devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teruel:
Teruel is a suffragan of Saragossa, covering the province except Bechi in Castellón. Some identify Teruel with ancient Turba, whose disputes with Saguntines gave Hannibal excuse to attack Saguntum. Teruel's annals place Turba not on the site but at its boundary. Sancho Sánchez Muñoz and Blasco Garcés Marcilla founded Teruel in 1176. It formed a community under the Fuero de Sepúlveda until 1598, when it came under Aragon.

Jaime I won its support for Valencia, and Teruel's standards waved in the Serranos gateway. In 1271 it joined war against Castile, invaded Huete and Cuenca, and backed Pedro IV. The king visited in 1348 and titled it exenta. Gregory XIII created the diocese in 1577 at Philip II's urging. The first bishop elected, Juan Pérez de Artieda, was never consecrated; the first installed, Andrés Santos, moved to Saragossa in 1579. Founders built nine churches, the central one becoming cathedral in 1577.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-arunde:
Thomas Arundel, sixtieth Archbishop of Canterbury, was born in 1353, the second son of the Earl of Arundel and Warren. Promoted to Ely while still in his early twenties, he became chancellor in 1386, moved to York in 1388, and reached Canterbury in 1396. Richard II soon attainted him for treason and sent him into exile in France and Rome.

Henry IV restored him to Canterbury in 1399, declaring his successor Roger Walden a usurper. Arundel is best remembered for his hard stand against the Lollards, pressing Rome to condemn their teaching and defending transubstantiation and papal authority. He died on 19 February 1414, after a career spent at the meeting point of church and crown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tower-of-babe:
The Tower of Babel is the building named in Genesis 11. Noah's descendants, spreading from the east into the plain of Shinar, resolved to build a city and a tower reaching heaven, to make their name famous before scattering. They used brick for stone and asphalt for mortar, but God confused their speech so they could no longer understand one another, and they left off building.

No Babylonian document yet found refers clearly to the tower, the entry notes. Smith, Sayce and others thought they had found allusions, but Delitzsch showed the key words too uncertain to prove it. The Talmud links Borsippa with the confusion of tongues, but the biblical account puts the tower inside city limits. Its form likely matched Babylonian staged towers, with shrinking blocks of masonry and stairs between storeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urgel:
Urgel is a Spanish diocese, suffragan of Tarragona. It is bounded on the north by France and on the east, south, and west by the provinces of Gerona, Barcelona, Lérida, and Huesca, with the valleys of Andorra. Its capital, Seo de Urgel, stands in northern Lérida between the Segre and Balira rivers and counts 4,000 inhabitants. The city ranks among Spain's most ancient, belonging to the Ilergetes and appearing on Iberian coins as Orgia or Orgelia.

Christianity reached Urgel very early. St Justus, its bishop, attended the Second Council of Toledo in 527 and the First Council of Lérida in 546, and wrote on the Canticle of Canticles for Sergius, Archbishop of Tarragona. The entry follows the see's bishops, its cathedral, and its mountain parishes through later centuries, a compact history of a Pyrenean diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentin-stan:
Valentin Stansel was an astronomer born at Olmütz in Moravia in 1621, who died at Bahia in Brazil on 18 December 1705. He joined the Society of Jesus on 1 October 1637 and taught rhetoric and mathematics at Olmütz and Prague. After ordination he asked to serve on the Jesuit mission in India and went to Portugal to await a ship, lecturing on astronomy with much success at the college of Évora meanwhile.

In Portugal he reshaped his name to Estancel, the form found on most of his published works. Obstacles blocked his passage to India, so he was sent to Brazil instead. He joined the Jesuit College and Seminary of San Salvador at Bahia as professor of moral theology and later of mathematics. The entry lists his astronomical writings, including observations of comets made from Brazil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-espin:
Vincent Espinel was a Spanish poet and novelist who lived from 1544 to 1634. Born at Ronda, he studied at Salamanca, served as a soldier in Italy and Flanders, took holy orders, and became chaplain of Ronda's hospital.

In 1618 he published at Barcelona a romance of Spanish manners, Relations of the Life and Deeds of Squire Marcos de Obregón. Admired at the time and later famous for its imitations and controversies, its hero's adventures thought largely drawn from Espinel's own life. Admirably written, full of wise maxims in pure, simple language, it was accused of supplying Le Sage with incidents and characters for Gil Blas. As poet he translated Horace's Art of Poetry, published his own verses in 1591, invented the ten-syllable décima stanza, and added a fifth string to the guitar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-tempe:
Wilhelm Tempel was a German sky-watcher who rose from lithographer to noted comet hunter without formal training. Born near Löbau in Saxony in 1821, he died near Florence in 1889. After a hard youth spent as sexton, gardener, and fee collector, he learned lithography, spent three years in Denmark, and settled in Venice around 1850, where he married and became a Catholic.

Venice friends stirred his love of the stars, and with a small comet-seeker he found a comet and the Merope Nebula in 1859. Paris shut its observatory to him for lack of schooling, but Marseilles took him on as an assistant in 1860. Working from windows and gardens, he went on to spot thirteen comets and four minor planets in ten years, and he published his sightings in the Astronomische Nachrichten.
christie-johnstone-a-novel:
Charles Reade built his novel Christie Johnstone around a bored lord whom pleasure has stopped pleasing. Viscount Ipsden, aged twenty-five with a large income, drifts through London and Europe hunting amusement. A doctor orders a cure: relieve one distressed person each day, and no more than one. The prescription sends the lord looking for work for his money and his heart.

Scotland gives the cure its setting, where Ipsden meets Christie Johnstone, a herring seller with a quick tongue and a creel to empty. Her plain speech and hard day's labor shame his soft hands and empty hours. Lady Barbara Sinclair, brilliant and political, offers the polished opposite pole of his old world. Reade, who dated the story to 1850 and refused to retouch it, mixes dialect comedy with social satire. Readers meet an early Reade here: energetic, funny, and preaching that labor dignifies life more than rank does.
darkness-and-daylight-a-novel:
Mary Jane Holmes opens Darkness and Daylight at Collingwood, a gloomy stone house empty for twelve years. Its owner wanders foreign lands, muttering of the darkness that fell when he lost his young wife. His son Richard has given up his youth to his father's whims. A fearful blight, blindness, is stealing upon noble Richard.

Edith Hastings comes to Collingwood as the story's daylight. Grace Atherton, Arthur, and the mystery at Grassy Spring fill the middle chapters. Nina, a strange childlike girl, carries the book's pathos. The darkness deepens, partings follow, and a fiery test prepares the sacrifice. A bridal and a leap of six years close the tale. Holmes was among America's best-selling domestic novelists, and this long novel shows her machinery of sentiment at full power.
democracy-an-american-novel:
Henry Adams published this novel anonymously in March 1880, and the prefatory note here records that his name reached the title page only in 1925. Readers of the first editions guessed at the author and at the real originals of the characters. The heroine needs no guessing: Mrs. Lightfoot Lee, a young New York widow, decides to pass a winter in Washington because New York has bored her into philosophy and philanthropy.

In Washington she sets out to understand the republic's working machinery at close range. A corrupt, charming senator from the West becomes her guide and her test. Adams builds the novel from drawing-room talk about power, money, and motive, and lets his widow ask the naive questions insiders avoid. It remains the sharpest short novel of Washington politics of its century.

This report develops a security licensing basis framework — the formal yardstick for judging a plant's defenses. A clear framework means no surprises when new reactor designs face review.
doe-osti-3377683-ssr-applied-automated-p: SSR APPLIED got V.2-automated, and this DOE text covers intelligent plants. The pages detail the efficient findings. The energy folks get their data. The digitised was automated. The data were energy. The V.2 were digitised. The efficient were intelligent.
doe-osti-3378007-fracture-analysis-of-co: Layered composite parts can peel apart from the inside — delamination — especially when built-in stresses pull at them. This work analyzes cohesive zone models, a math tool for predicting how such fractures grow. Better fracture analysis means lighter, safer composite designs.
doe-osti-3395398-bldg-7930-cell-g-neutro: Bldg 7930 got detector-electronicked, and this DOE text tests new electronics. The pages detail the neutron findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The cell was G. The data were nuclear. The electronics were new. The 7930 were Bldg. The neutron were detector.
doe-osti-3547200-gms-coi-data-model: GMS COI got data-modeled, and this DOE model covers the COI data. The pages detail the GMS findings. The computing folks get their data. The model was data. The data were computing. The COI were GMS. The data were computing.
doe-osti-3874833-l2-report-on-the-local-: LWN got L2-reported, and this DOE report covers the local wavenumber model. The pages detail the L2 findings. The physicists get their data. The model was wavenumber. The data were physicist. The L2 were local. The wavenumber were model.
doe-osti-3874843-differentiable-plant-hy: Plants got sapfluxnet-differentiated, and this DOE model covers hydrodynamic training. The pages detail the differentiable findings. The climate folks get their data. The observations were global. The data were climate. The sapfluxnet were training. The global were observations. The hydrodynamic were model.
doe-osti-3943093-a-hybrid-approach-to-co: Constitutive models got hybrid-discovered, and this DOE approach covers coupled physics fusion. The pages detail the hybrid findings. The engineers get their data. The fusion was multi-modal. The data were engineer. The multi-modal were data. The coupled were physics.
el-dorado-an-adventure-of-the-scarlet-pi: El Dorado, an adventure of the Scarlet Pimpernel by Baroness Orczy. The hero's Paris rescue. This book preserves that adventure. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
essays-of-travel:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Essays of Travel, printed in 1905, gathers his wandering prose from Scotland, France, and America. The longest piece, The Amateur Emigrant, records his 1879 crossing from the Clyde to Sandy Hook in steerage and second cabin. He describes steerage scenes and types, the sick man, stowaways, and his arrival in New York.

Shorter essays walk through Cockermouth and Keswick, an autumn effect, a winter's walk in Carrick and Galloway, and forest notes on Fontainebleau. Stevenson traveled to learn people as much as places, and his judgments stay personal and exact. Together the pieces show the essayist who would later write the great South Seas and California books.
frederick-the-great-and-his-family-a-his:
Luise Mühlbach wrote Frederick the Great and His Family, a historical novel of Prussia translated from German by Mrs Chapman Coleman and her daughters. Frederick rules Prussia at the height of his fame. His brothers, courtiers, and enemies fill a court built on discipline and suspicion. Baron Trenck, the daring officer Frederick imprisoned, threads through the plot.

Three books of chapters move from masked balls and secret captains to open war. Trenck travels toward prison, flees, and returns in disguise. Prince Henry and his unhappy wife carry the family drama. Battles, including Collin, and the capture of Dresden's archives widen the canvas. Gellert the poet faces the king in one famous scene. Readers get a long, romantic version of Frederick's reign, mixing documented events with invented love stories and escapes.
frontinus-aqueducts-herschel:
Clemens Herschel translated Frontinus's account of Rome's aqueducts in editions of 1899 and 1913. Sextus Julius Frontinus served as Rome's water commissioner around 100 CE. His official report, De Aquaeductu, is the classic of hydraulic engineering.

Frontinus lists each aqueduct's source, length, and delivery in exact figures. He exposes water theft, illegal taps, and sloppy maintenance by his staff. Repairs, water quality, and the law of water rights all receive chapters. Herschel was himself a practicing hydraulic engineer, which shows in the notes. Bureaucracy rarely reads this well or this honestly. Engineers still study how Rome delivered water to a million people.
govdocs-archive_org-SatanicRitualSitesUS: Scanned pages of a work cataloguing alleged satanic ritual sites across the United States make up this file, with pictures of the sites included. The scan is heavily garbled, and much of the text cannot be recovered from it, so the substance of the original work is largely lost. The author is not identified in the record. It is kept as found, a damaged piece of the era's ritual-abuse literature whose images and fragments still show what the original set out to document.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AbelowMartin_Ru:
Nine months after the Kennedy assassination, the FBI was still working its files on Lee Harvey Oswald. This document, dated August 1964 and numbered 105-37111, is part of that continuing Bureau record on the accused assassin.

It concerns Oswald's alleged leafleting for the Fair Play for Cuba Committee in New Orleans, where he had handed out pro-Castro literature in the summer of 1963. It also takes up allegations that advance knowledge of the assassination plot existed somewhere. Such memos show the FBI chasing the loose ends of Oswald's Cuban connections long after the Warren Commission's work began.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIARayManuel_CI:
Manuel Ray was a Cuban exile leader who had broken with both Castro and the CIA-backed exile establishment. Charles Bartlett, writing in the Chicago Sun-Times on July 27, 1961, covered Ray's public attack on CIA intervention in Cuban exile politics.

Three months after the Bay of Pigs failure, the exile movement was at war with itself, and Ray's charge was that the agency's hand in exile affairs was ruining the cause. The column's headline, Cuban CIA Critic Sealing Own Fate, gives Bartlett's judgment on what such candor would cost Ray. The article is preserved as post-invasion journalism from the exile fight.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GilManuel_Gil_M:
Harold Weisberg sent Jim Garrison a memorandum on March 17, 1966 about a man named Manuel Gil. The memo covers Gil and his associates. It also takes up the Bringuier propaganda distribution and the DRE, the Cuban student exile group active in New Orleans.

Weisberg fed Garrison leads as the district attorney built his case, and this memo is that traffic in writing. Carlos Bringuier's group had clashed publicly with Lee Harvey Oswald in 1963. A memo mapping Gil's circle and the propaganda work preserves the researcher's view of the exile scene Garrison was entering.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HurwitzMichael_: Michael Hurwitz wrote to Harold Weisberg on April 5, 1992. By then Weisberg had been receiving researchers' letters for three decades, and his files grew with each one. The surviving record gives the writer, the recipient, and the date but no subject, so the entry stands as a dated letter into the assassination researcher's mailbox.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JamesDaniel_Jam: A garbled letter protests the FBI's handling of Freedom of Information Act appeals. The writer, who is not identified, charges that delays and withholdings in the appeals process amount to a way of negating compliance with the law. The text is damaged, but its complaint is clear: an appeal answered too late, or emptied of records, is a refusal by another name.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MajerusMichael_: A fragment of a handwritten letter survives here, mentioning years of research and works including 'Accessories After the Fact,' an early critical book on the Kennedy case. The handwriting and the scan defeat full reading: the author's name and the letter's full subject cannot be recovered. What remains is evidence of the letter-writing traffic among assassination researchers, most of it now lost, of which this scrap is a sample.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarshMichael_Ma:
Michael Marsh lectured on the Kennedy assassination in the 1970s, and audiences wrote back. This file holds fan letters from 1977 thanking him for his talks. One came from a Winthrop College student, dated October 19, 1977, after a campus appearance.

Lecture circuits carried the assassination debate across the country in those years, hall by hall. A speaker brought slides, documents, and an argument; listeners answered with letters like these. They show what reached people: not the full evidence, but a case made in an evening. The letters also record names, dates, and places, the paper trail of a traveling lecturer and the audiences who thought he was right.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MowerEdgarAnsel: Chalmers M. Roberts reviewed two memoirs for the Washington Post under the title 'Panoramas of Our Times.' One memoir was by Arthur Krock, the longtime New York Times columnist. The other was by Edgar Ansel Mowrer, a foreign correspondent. Reviewers paired such books because both men had watched decades of public life from inside the press. The file gives the pairing and the headline, but not the review's judgments.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PierceSamuel_Pi: From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers. An obscure item, complete, filed. A bare file, kept as issued. Subject: government records. nsia-PierceSamuel Pierce Samuel: the made public government document, captured as titled.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Dep:
The State Department's Dissent Channel lets Foreign Service officers formally protest policy without ending their careers. This briefing book reveals historic messages sent through that channel. The protests cover some of the darkest episodes of the era.

Officers protested American inaction over the My Lai atrocities, which one compared to those of the Nazis. Others charged selective genocide in Bangladesh and Burundi. One message accused officials of cooking the books on Vietnam intelligence. Still others challenged policy toward the Soviet Union and China. Read together, the cables prove that dissent inside government was written down and filed, not just felt.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_human-ri:
In 1989 Salvadoran soldiers murdered six Jesuit priests and two women who worked with them. Kate Doyle and Peter Kornbluh edited this Spanish-language Archive publication, titled CULPABLE, meaning guilty. It concerns the long campaign for justice in that case.

Its companion English briefing book covers the Spanish court verdict against Colonel Montano. This Spanish edition carries the same accountability story to the language of the country where the murders happened. Evidence here gives the editors and subject only, so the set is best described plainly: an Archive publication on justice for the Jesuits of El Salvador.

Six Jesuit priests, their housekeeper, and her daughter were murdered by Salvadoran soldiers in 1989. Kate Doyle and Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 713, published in July 2020. It reports a Spanish court holding Colonel Inocente Orlando Montano accountable for the massacre.

Spain used universal jurisdiction, the principle that some crimes can be tried anywhere. A Salvadoran officer was thus convicted of state terror in a Madrid courtroom, decades after the killings. The Archive hailed the verdict in the Jesuit case. The record shows one path to justice when a home country will not prosecute its own officers.
hebbel-three-plays-by-frederic-hebbel:
Three tragedies by Friedrich Hebbel introduce English readers to the brooding North German dramatist in this translated selection. Hebbel's plays pit single souls against the crushing machinery of history and morality. His characters are often destroyed by the very ideas they serve most faithfully.

The selected tragedies test purity, honor, and faith against worlds that cannot hold their heroes. Hebbel saw tragedy in the collision of old orders with new ones. The selection gives English readers a fair doorway into a difficult master. Nineteenth-century Germany produced no sterner dramatic intelligence. Those who enter Hebbel's world rarely leave it unshaken, or unchanged in how they read Ibsen after.
henry-dunbar-a-novel: Henry Dunbar, a novel by Mary Elizabeth Braddon. Its Victorian tale unfolds. This book preserves that novel. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
henry-viii-and-his-court-a-historical-no:
Luise Mühlbach wrote Henry VIII and His Court as a historical novel of Tudor England, translated from German by H N Pierce. The action begins in 1543, on the day Henry marries his sixth wife. Catharine Parr, young widow of Baron Latimer, walks to the altar pale with fear. Bishops Gardiner and Cranmer attend her. She knows what happened to the wives before her.

Court intrigue surrounds the new queen from her wedding day. Enemies plot to brand her a heretic, as they destroyed Catharine Howard before her. Thomas Seymour's rash loyalty complicates her position. Mühlbach fills palaces with ceremony, whispered accusations, and rival churchmen. Readers get a German novelist's dramatic version of Henry's last marriage, where a queen's learning and faith could cost her life at any careless word.
hilgers-der-index-der-verbotenen-bucher-: Der Index der verbotenen Bücher, in seiner neuen Fassung, by Hilgers. The banned-books index. This book preserves that study. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
james-pethel:
Max Beerbohm begins James Pethel by reading his subject's sudden death in a newspaper over breakfast, and admitting the shock was not wholly disagreeable. Pethel was a mere acquaintance, a wealthy man the narrator knew slightly through country-house society. The story reconstructs him from meetings, gossip, and one long-remembered visit.

Pethel made a fortune, married, and glittered briefly, yet the narrator keeps finding something hollow behind the success. A pale wife and a daughter with her hair still down unsettle his memories of the man's prime. Beerbohm's prose stays silken and cruel by turns, turning a slight acquaintance into a study of worldly success and its quiet failure to satisfy.
joseph-ii-and-his-court-an-historical-no:
L. Muhlbach wrote this historical novel of the Austrian court, and Adelaide DeV. Chaudron translated it from the German. The story centers on Joseph, son and heir of the Empress Maria Theresa, and on the ministers and rivals who surround the throne in Vienna. Its opening chapters sit in on the empress's council, where her trusted lords expect her to renew old treaties and keep the court's settled course.

The book moves through the young archduke's marriage to Isabella of Parma, court opera under Gluck, and the feuds of ministers such as Kaunitz and Bartenstein. Muhlbach mixes real rulers and courtiers with invented talk and private scenes, so readers get a full, dramatized picture of how power, marriage, and ambition worked at the Habsburg court.
kate-danton-or-captain-danton-s-daughter:
Kate Danton, or Captain Danton's Daughters is a novel by May Agnes Fleming, printed at Toronto in 1877. Fleming wrote many popular novels, including Norine's Revenge, A Terrible Secret, and A Mad Marriage. Two mottoes open the book, one on a woman's will dying hard. The other sings of three little women weaving pleasant thoughts with their lace.

Those three women, the poem hints, think all the while of three little men. The poem names the robin, the wood dove, and the wren among its birds. Fleming sets her story of the captain's daughters inside that frame of courtship and will. The Toronto edition came from Belford Brothers, printed by the Globe Printing Company. It is Canadian popular fiction of the 1870s, aimed at eager general readers.
katrine-a-novel:
Katrine is a novel by Elinor Macartney Lane, published by Harper and Brothers in 1909. Its dedication is a verse addressed to Grant B. Schley, dated from Paris in 1909. The contents open under the Southern pines, with a meeting in the woods. A promise made in the rose garden follows, and the Frenchman's creek appears in chapter six.

Frank falls further under Katrine's influence, as one title plainly says. At Dermott's dinner party he becomes distrait, and later he yields to temptation. Mr. Ravenel and a ballroom conversation draw the threads tighter. A story in a graveyard and a place called Ravenel stand late in the list. Lane writes a Southern romance of love, money, and tested honor around her heroine.
kitty-canary-a-novel:
Kate Langley Bosher, author of Mary Cary, wrote the novel Kitty Canary. Harper and Brothers held its copyright from 1913, and this printing appeared in 1918. Kitty herself tells the story in the first person.

Kitty opens by announcing that she is in love. She is boarding for the summer in another woman's house. The man she loves was once engaged to that woman's niece, Elizabeth. Kitty tells the tale with humor, spirit, and sharp remarks about people who stay easily hurt. Kitty's voice is the book's chief charm from the first page. She judges others sharply, yet her own heart keeps surprising her.
leah-mordecai-a-novel:
Belle Kendrick Abbott wrote Leah Mordecai, a novel set in a fashionable girls' school. She dedicated it to her uncle, the Reverend J. Ryland Kendrick. His hospitable home, she says, brightened her young life.

The first chapter opens at Madam Truxton's school at dismissal hour. Groups of restless, anxious pupils wait in the assembly room. A giant clock on the wall marks the hour. Leah stands at the center of the schoolgirl world Abbott builds. Family, faith, and young ambition shape the story that follows. Abbott wrote from Atlanta, and Southern settings ground the tale. School discipline and home faith pull Leah in different directions.
life-of-john-coleridge-patteson-missiona:
Charlotte Mary Yonge wrote this life of Bishop Patteson. John Coleridge Patteson served as missionary bishop of the Melanesian Islands. Yonge notes the advantages of writing while memories stay fresh. Contemporaries could still certify facts that hearsay would soon blur.

She also warns that results of his actions remain unclear. Patteson died comparatively young, with his harvest barely gathered. Many people woven into his life were still active then. The biography preserves a recently lost missionary's story for his church. Seclusion marked the later part of his subject's short career. Yonge asks readers to weigh sowing against an ungathered harvest.
lo-michael:
Grace Livingston Hill opens this novel amid a crowd of urchins. A biblical verse from Daniel supplies its title and epigraph. Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help, it reads. A voice shouts a warning to little Mikky in chapter one.

The child flashes past the huddled group without heeding. Twenty-nine chapters carry Michael's story forward from the streets. Hill wrote many such inspirational novels for popular readers. Faith and rescue shape the plot her epigraph announces. Daniel chapter ten, verse thirteen supplies the exact wording. Mikky's opening danger sets Hill's rescue plot moving immediately.
louisa-of-prussia-and-her-times-a-histor:
Louisa of Prussia and Her Times is a historical novel by Luise Mühlbach. It was translated from the German by F. Jordan. The book belongs to her Napoleon in Germany series. It opens with the Treaty of Campo Formio and dreadful tidings in Vienna.

Readers meet the composer Joseph Haydn and the young General Bonaparte. Then the story turns to Prussia and its young queen, Louisa. Her wedding and early court years fill the middle chapters. Napoleon shadows her short and tragic life from afar. Mühlbach mixes real events with deep feeling for her heroine. The novel became a tender tribute to a much-loved queen.
love-s-pilgrimage-a-novel:
Love's Pilgrimage is a novel by Upton Sinclair, the muckraking American writer. Its contents divide the story into Love's Entanglement and Love's Captivity. Book titles speak of a victim, a snare, and bait seized. The tale opens in a little woodland glen with a tumbling streamlet.

What begins as woodland romance hardens into a trap, in Sinclair's telling. Later books name a torture-house, a treadmill, and masters of the snare. The captive's cords tighten until a break for freedom comes. Sinclair turns a love story into a charge against marriage without freedom. It is among his most personal and bitter novels.
lying-prophets-a-novel:
Lying Prophets is a novel by Eden Phillpotts, the Devon and Dartmoor writer. Its epigraph gives the title in broad West Country dialect. One man took plain Nature for God, and talked foolishness of flowers and bees. Another set God by the mouth of hell, laughing at the damned.

'They be lying prophets — lying prophets both,' the speaker concludes. Book One, called Art, opens near Newlyn, in a white cottage over low cliffs. Orchards slope behind it, and the sea laps below. Phillpotts sets false faiths against the real lives of Cornish folk. The novel asks what a true picture of God would be.
mare-nostrum-our-sea-a-novel:
Mare Nostrum, Our Sea, is a novel by Vicente Blasco Ibáñez. Charlotte Brewster Jordan translated it from the Spanish in 1919. Ibáñez had lately won world fame with The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. His hero is Captain Ulysses Ferragut, a Mediterranean sailor.

Chapters name Mater Amphitrite and Pater Oceanus, mother and father of his sea. In Naples and Marseilles, Ferragut falls under the wiles of Circe. The enchantress is Freya, a beautiful agent of wartime intrigue. His young son plays Telemachus to this wandering Ulysses. Love draws the neutral captain toward Germany's secret war. The novel mixes sea romance with the spy fever of 1914.
memoir-and-diary-of-john-yeardley-minist:
Charles Tylor edited the Memoir and Diary of John Yeardley. Henry Longstreth printed it in Philadelphia in 1860. Yeardley was a minister of the gospel, as the title states.

Chapter one runs from his conversion to his ministry's start in 1815. He joins the Society of Friends and weds Elizabeth Dunn. His diary starts in those years, and trade work fills his days. Chapter two takes him to a call to live and work in Germany in 1820. His trade failed even as his preaching grew in strength. The diary lets readers track that strain in his own words.
michael:
E. F. Benson's novel follows Michael Comber, a rich young man with a clumsy, ungainly body. The first scene shows his gift for giving: he cheerfully writes a cheque for his indebted cousin Francis. Michael asks only that Francis write within two days confirming the bills are paid. His generosity, everyone agrees, is entirely genuine.

Yet Michael feels cheap because he never misses what he gives away. Benson builds the story around that tension between wealth and real sacrifice. Around Michael move cousins and friends who accept his kindness gracefully or exploit it. The novel studies Edwardian manners and one man's artistic, sensitive nature in fine, ironic detail.
mike-fletcher-a-novel:
George Moore published this novel in 1889, dedicating it to his brother Augustus. The opening scene fills Lubini's famous London restaurant with noise and color. Women in silk skirts and opera cloaks push through the swing doors. Thirty faultlessly dressed throats roar for brandies and sodas at the bar.

Beyond the bar, a narrow gallery holds supping couples and sharp smells of savories and patchouli. Moore piles up sense impressions in the new naturalist manner. The scene introduces the bohemian London world his characters inhabit. Readers meet a young literary set through its restaurants, talk, and late-night energy.
miriam-monfort-a-novel:
Catherine A. Warfield, author of The Household of Bouverie, published this novel with D. Appleton in New York in 1873. She dedicated it to the memory of one who watched the book grow. Its epigraphs quote Browning's Ring and the Book on fancy and fact. A prefatory poem, Monfort Hall, speaks of a dark spirit walking in the house.

The poem's speaker describes being lured from a calm asylum toward an abyss. Such omens set the tone for a tale of destiny closing on a household. Warfield, a Southern novelist, wrote in the romantic mode her readers expected. The novel mixes family drama with fate and foreboding.
nancy-a-novel:
Rhoda Broughton published this novel with Appleton in New York in 1874. She had written Good-bye, Sweetheart and Red as a Rose Is She. A Tennyson verse about a husband and wife fronts the tale. Chapter one opens in a kitchen, mid-recipe.

Butter melts in a small preserving pan for brown sugar candy. Algy insists the browner the sugar, the better. Bobby calls brown sugar filthy stuff, and the brothers spar. Nancy reads the recipe aloud, fast and dull, to stop the fight. Broughton's lively talk and sharp young voices made her a star of the sensation age.
napoleon-and-blu-cher-an-historical-nove:
Luise Mühlbach wrote this historical novel of the wars against Napoleon. The Prussian marshal Blücher shares the stage with the French emperor. Mühlbach was famed in Germany for novels built on real courts and camps. Her books reached English readers in wide translation.

The tale dramatizes the great struggle that broke Napoleon's power. Hard war and bold strategy drive the narrative, as V1 sums it. Blücher's stout, forward style made him the people's hero of the fight. Mühlbach blends letters, speeches, and battle scenes into her story. The result is popular history in novel form, stirring and rich in period color.
nasa-tm-19640023715-computation-of-the-m:
Joseph C. Cain, Shirley Hendricks, Walter E. Daniels, and Duane C. Jensen wrote this paper in October 1964. It computes Earth's main magnetic field from spherical harmonic expansions. That math describes a round world's field as a sum of smooth patterns. Each pattern adds finer detail to the whole.

A good field model serves navigation, science, and satellite work. Compasses, ore surveys, and space weather studies all lean on it. The authors turn global field measures into a working computation. V1 notes this toolkit was the standard approach for the job. The paper helped fix the reference field that later models of Earth's magnetism built upon.
nasa-tm-19660018733-investigation-of-the:
E L Shriver, in Marshall's Research Projects Laboratory, tested a way to measure electric field strength with a beam of electrons in this April 12, 1966, report. An electric field bends the path of a moving electron. Watching that bend can reveal how strong the field is. Shriver's meter works across a low range of field strengths, the abstract states.

A direct meter for weak fields serves work on plasmas and on charged spacecraft. Fields in space are faint, yet they steer particles and affect instruments. Beam deflection gives a reading tied to a visible movement, not a faint current alone. Shriver investigates whether the method is practical as a measuring tool, and how far its range can reach.
nasa-tm-19670009026-astrophysical-eviden:
Chao-wen Chin, Hong-Yee Chiu, and Richard Stothers wrote this paper at NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. A summary was presented at a theoretical physics conference at Stony Brook in November 1965. Their subject is astrophysical evidence for the direct weak interaction between electrons and neutrinos.

Neutrinos interact so weakly that laboratory proof was hard to get. The authors look for evidence in stars instead. The catalog record says they use theoretical models of unusually bright white dwarfs. Those models are built with and without a neutrino emission process, so the two versions can be compared against observation.
nasa-tm-19670025784-force-measurements-o:
Bruno J. Gambucci and Robert C. Robinson, of NASA's Ames Research Center in California, ran wind-tunnel tests reported in August 1967. Their models were axisymmetric bodies with hammerhead noses, blunt fronts wider than the body behind them. Such shapes appear on missiles and space vehicles.

The team measured normal-force, pitching-moment, and axial-force values for five models. Tests covered the transonic range, from Mach 0.70 to Mach 1.20. Angles of attack stayed small, a few degrees either way. The resulting data set let designers predict how hammerhead shapes behave near the speed of sound.
nasa-tm-19680012181-simultaneous-measure:
D. H. Fairfield, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, caught Earth's magnetic tail a thousand radii away in April 1968. During one week in September 1966, Pioneer 7 sat behind Earth in the tail's path. Explorer 28 and Explorer 33 watched the solar wind and the near-Earth sheath at the same time.

Comparing the three craft's magnetic readings isolates Pioneer 7's tail sightings. About ten intervals stand out, lasting minutes to hours. Fairfield reads them as the tail sweeping back and forth across the spacecraft. The tail swings as the solar wind changes direction. Field jumps also drift past all three craft at wind-like speeds.
nasa-tm-19690027373-numerical-research-f:
Iwao Hosokawa and Kiyoshi Yamamoto wrote this September 1969 preprint, numbered X-641-69-392, on the Burgers model of turbulence. The Burgers model is a one-dimensional stand-in for real turbulence, simple enough for exact statistical treatment. Their approach rests on the Hopf theory of statistical fluid mechanics, carried out with a high-speed computer.

They compute a functional integral expression for the velocity correlation function. The starting flow is assumed random, with a bell-shaped spread of speeds. Watching the energy decay curve shift as the Reynolds number grows implies one limiting curve at extreme values. Their correlation values also suggest a known spectrum law holds in one wave range. Both results guide tests of fuller turbulence theories.
nasa-tm-19700026568-description-and-gene:
The Measurement Systems Division at the Kennedy Space Center issued this guideline in June 1969. It describes the center's lightning warning system and tells how to run it. Document number GP-567 covers the system that guards the launch site.

Florida storms strike fast, and a loaded rocket on the pad is a prime lightning target. The guideline explains what the warning system does and how staff should work with it. It includes a list of the pages in force, so users know their copy is current. Such rules kept crews, rockets, and pad gear safe in storm season.
nasa-tm-19710005807-a-comparison-of-dwba:
R. J. Ascuitto of Yale University led this study, with Richard C. Braley and William F. Ford of the Lewis Research Center. They presented it at a physics meeting at Stanford in December 1970. It compares two ways to model particles scattering off nuclei in the 2s-1d shell.

One way, called DWBA, treats each scattering in a single step. The other, coupled channels, lets several nuclear states act on each other during the hit. The low states of these nuclei are strongly excited, the authors note. That fact argues for the fuller method, at least for some levels. Their comparison adjusts the simpler model fairly before judging the two.
nasa-tm-19710014175-a-sweep-gas-facility:
Thomas A Kirchgessner, Michael B Weinstein, and Thomas N Tambling of the Lewis Research Center described this new test facility in May 1971. It was built at the NASA Plum Brook Reactor in Ohio. The facility measures gases that escape from working nuclear fuel samples. Such release rates matter for designing fuel for space power reactors.

Helium sweep gas flows past a fuel sample and carries escaped gases to detectors. A scintillation detector reads the gas isotopes as the test runs. Staff can also draw samples for closer laboratory study. The facility ran well with mock and real fuel samples. Its working limit at the time reached three hundred watts of fission power.
nasa-tm-19710020579-lewis-9-by-15-foot-v:
Joseph A Yuska, James H Diedrich, and Nestor Clough described a new Lewis Research Center wind tunnel in July 1971. The nine by fifteen foot V/STOL tunnel was built inside the return leg of the eight by six foot supersonic tunnel. V/STOL aircraft rise or land vertically, then fly forward. Testing them needs a big test section with slow, steady air.

Air speed in the new tunnel ran from about thirty to one hundred seventy five miles per hour. The report describes the tunnel's features in full. It also presents the first calibration results in careful detail. Those results guide future users in planning their experiments. Appendixes explain the inlet, wall slot, and diffuser designs.
not-george-washington-an-autobiographica:
P. G. Wodehouse and Herbert Westbrook called Not George Washington an autobiographical novel, published in 1907. The tale is told by turns, in named narratives. Miss Margaret Goodwin opens part one, with James arriving, James setting out, and a harmless deception. James Orlebar Cloyster then takes up the story.

Cloyster's part covers an invasion of Bohemia, a secret, and three ghosts in a row. Sidney Price and Julian Eversleigh narrate later parts. A ghostly gathering, a man in the soup, and Norah winning home mark Price's share. Briggs comes to the rescue near the end, and triumph closes the book. Shifting voices give the comedy its pace.
oh-money-money-a-novel:
Eleanor Hodgman Porter wrote the novel Oh, Money! Money! She also wrote The Road to Understanding and Just David. Helen Mason Grose drew the pictures for the book. Chapter titles name Stanley Fulton and a Mr. John Smith. A Santa Claus figure appears more than once.

The early chapters move from Fulton to Smith and his kin. Cousins, dates, and an album drive parts of the plot. Poor Maggie appears as a figure of concern. Money and family duty seem central to the tale. Porter writes warm fiction about ordinary people and gifts. The contents run to at least twelve chapters of family scenes.
oriental-religions-and-christianity-a-co: Frank F. Ellinwood delivered the lectures in Oriental Religions and Christianity at Union Theological Seminary in New York in 1891. They were published in 1892. His subject is why missionaries and ministers should study the religions of Asia. The hosted sample shows only the contents. The long outline for the first lecture argues the need to understand what Ellinwood calls the false religions. It lists reasons from growing contact between nations to the awakening of Asian minds. No lecture text appears in the sample.
our-elizabeth-a-humour-novel:
Florence A. Kilpatrick first sketched her heroine in Punch. She then grew her to full life-size in Our Elizabeth, a humour novel published in London in November 1920. Her author's note insists Elizabeth is not a type. She is one person, a character apart. There is only one Elizabeth, the note says. Signs and omens at her birth, Kilpatrick jokes, fixed her streak of superstition.

Across nineteen chapters, Elizabeth Renshaw carries the comedy. The frontispiece pictures her in full charm. The note is the book's whole manifesto. Warm character comedy, built on one woman's fixed and funny view of the world, is the promise. Kilpatrick thanks the early sketches for Elizabeth's features. The novel offers the portrait at full scale.
our-unitarian-gospel:
Minot J. Savage preached the sermons in Our Unitarian Gospel at the Church of the Messiah in Boston. The season was 1897 to 1898. He printed them, his note says, not as literature. He wanted to preach to a larger congregation than a Sunday morning can hold. The dedication addresses those who believe God's message must be one of life and hope, not a theology of death and despair.

The sermon titles map his gospel: why Unitarians have no creed, whether any creed is wicked to question, sin and atonement, prayer, reward and punishment, and things which doubt cannot destroy. The first sermon attacks the notion that Unitarianism is a new-fangled fad. Like the Copernican theory, Savage says, newness would be nothing against it. But Unitarianism is not new at all; it is very old.
overland-a-novel:
John William De Forest, author of Miss Ravenel's Conversion, set his 1871 novel Overland in Santa Fé, New Mexico, and opens by abusing the place handsomely. Santa Fé is an undergrown, decrepit, out-at-elbows ancient hidalgo of a town. It is two hundred and seventy years old, with fewer than five thousand inhabitants. Sun-baked brick houses line its few narrow streets. The fine climate makes it difficult to die there. Everything else makes it almost as difficult to live.

Emigrants halt there to refit and always resolutely start on again. The wonder of the opening is a couple of newcomers on a flat roof: the handsomest girl in Santa Fé, and beside her a remarkable woman very sure of her own remarkableness. De Forest, the most realistic American novelist of his generation, launches his love story overland from that roof.
people-like-that-a-novel:
Kate Langley Bosher, author of Mary Cary, published People Like That in 1916. Her narrator is an unrequired person of twenty-six with an income sufficient for necessities. Having the right to choose where she lives, she chooses Scarborough Square, and her friends and relatives are scandalized.

The square is the last square of respectability in a forgotten part of town. The narrator likes heading her own half-house there, and refuses to explain herself. The novel watches what happens when a comfortable young woman moves among people her own class would never visit, and what she learns from them.
phantom-fortune-a-novel: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Phantom Fortune, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page gives the author only as the author of Lady Audley's Secret and Vixen, meaning M. E. Braddon. The contents open with Penelope and Ulysses, pass through forty years after and a skeleton in the family. They promise Lady Maulevrier's letter-bag, the dark brow of Helvellyn, a character named Lesbia, and a lord who refuses a fortune.
phantom-wires-a-novel: A hosted sample showing only the front matter of Phantom Wires, the title pages, copyright pages, and two short motto verses, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Arthur Stringer, author of The Wire Tappers. Illustrations are by Arthur William Brown. Little, Brown published it at Boston, with copyright in 1907 and 1908. The motto verses play on the bad in the best of us and the muddle of hope and madness that makes up humanity.
pontoppidan-lykke-per-frste-del:
Henrik Pontoppidan begins Lucky Per, his great Danish novel, with this first part in the original Danish. Per Sidenius, a clever young engineer, breaks with his clergyman father's strict faith. He aims to conquer modern Denmark with talent, plans, and sheer will.

Per leaves home for study, work, and love in a changing land. Ambition lifts him, yet pride and restlessness shadow each gain he makes. Pontoppidan, who shared the Nobel Prize in 1917, writes with cool irony. The opening sets up a full life story: a gifted man against family, church, and his own flaws.
poor-white-a-novel:
Sherwood Anderson published Poor White in 1920, the year after Winesburg, Ohio made his name, dedicating the novel to Tennessee Mitchell Anderson. Its hero, Hugh McVey, is born in a miserable town on a mud bank of the Mississippi in Missouri, a place river men mockingly called Mudcat Landing. Where the soil is yellow, shallow, and stony, the farmers gaunt and discouraged, the merchants unpaid, and only the two saloons prosper, since they alone sell for cash.

Hugh's father, a failed tannery hand turned drunkard, and his dead mother set the boy's start. The novel follows his escape north and his rise as an inventor in an Ohio town being remade by industry. Anderson asks what the machine age does to the poor white stock it lifts up. Less famous than Winesburg, the novel shares its compassion and its target: the spiritual cost of American getting ahead.
precaution-a-novel:
James Fenimore Cooper's first novel, Precaution, appears here fronted by William Cullen Bryant's discourse on Cooper's life. Genius, and writings, delivered at Metropolitan Hall in New York in February 1852, months after Cooper's death. Bryant opens in grief: a year earlier Cooper's friends were planning a public dinner in his honor. Now they assemble for the sadder purpose of paying the dead the honors meant for the living, to vacancy and silence.

The memoir traces the making of the novelist, from his father building the first house in Cooperstown in 1786 on the borders of Otsego Lake. Praises Cooper's magnanimous frankness and refusal of deceit. Precaution itself, an English-set novel of manners written on a dare, is the least characteristic Cooper. Yet the frame makes the volume a monument: America's first great novelist, mourned by its first great poet, with the apprentice work attached.
queed-a-novel: Queed is a novel by Henry Sydnor Harrison, published by Houghton Mifflin Company in 1911 with a frontispiece by R. M. Crosby and a dedication to the author's mother. Only the title pages and contents are shown. The chapter headings promise a boarding-house tale: a first meeting with Charles Gardiner West, Mrs. Paynter's boarding-house, Charlotte Lee Weyland pressing Doctor Queed for his unpaid board, and Queed taking work under Colonel Cowles.
quiet-talks-on-john-s-gospel:
Quiet Talks on John's Gospel, by S. D. Gordon, dated 1915, reads the fourth Gospel as a story of wooing. Its seven parts move from John's Story through The Wooing Lover. The Lover Wooing comes next. Then comes the greatest wooing of the passion. Two meetings after the resurrection close the book. One is a surprise. One is a breakfast by the Sea of Galilee.

Chapter one opens by quoting the poem of flight. "I fled Him, down the nights and down the days" sets the book's frame. A lover pursues the soul. He sups with open hearts in moonlight and shadow. He meets hard hearts with tender passion before the tragedy.
richard-vandermarck-a-novel:
Mrs. Sidney S. Harris, author of Rutledge and St. Phillips, published this novel in 1871, dedicated to S. S. H. Its title names its hero, Richard Vandermarck, and its contents open on Varick-Street. Very Good Luck and a chapter named Kilian follow, then My Companions and The Tutor.

Matinal and Three Weeks Too Late mark the middle chapters, with Sunday and A Dance for social scenes. Every Day from Six to Seven suggests a standing appointment kept or missed. Sophie's Work enters near the close of the list shown, and a Latin warning, Praemonitus, Praemunitus — forewarned, forearmed — heads the twelfth chapter.
round-the-block-an-american-novel: John Bell Bouton wrote Round the Block, an American novel with pictures, dated 1864. A front picture shows Mrs. Slapman at home. The contents divide the book into parts, with Book First called New Year's Day and Book Second called Polishing. Early chapters include The Block, Three Bachelors, Peeps, Quigg, Pleasure as Business, Something Hidden, The Boy Bog, and Mrs. Slapman at Home. Book Second opens with The Enigma, A Delicate Proposition, Miss Pillbody, and A Friend in Need.
rudin-a-novel:
Ivan Turgenev wrote Rudin, a novel translated from the Russian by Constance Garnett and issued in London in 1894 by William Heinemann. An introduction by S. Stepniak opens the volume. Stepniak argues that Turgenev no longer belongs to Russia only. In the last fifteen years of his life Turgenev won readers first in France, then in Germany and America, and at last in England. At his funeral, Ernest Renan hailed him for the French as one of the greatest writers of the age.

Stepniak stresses that this fame grew slowly, with none of the sudden rush that lifted Count Tolstoi to world fame in a few years. Nothing in Turgenev's person or talent, he says, struck and swept away the crowd at once. His strength lay in making people. Stepniak praises the vast gallery of living men, and above all women, each distinct and true to life.
run-to-earth-a-novel: Run to Earth, a novel headed with the year 1867 and the name Braddon, M. E., is billed only as by the author of Lady Audley's Secret, Aurora Floyd, Ishmael, Vixen, and Wyllard's Weird. A front picture shows Honoria murmuring that she is in the power of a maniac. The contents list twenty-six chapters, opening with Warned in a Dream, Done in the Darkness, Disinherited, and Out of the Depths.
rung-ho-a-novel: Talbot Mundy wrote Rung Ho, headed as a novel from 1914. The contents page lists the title piece, Rung Ho, followed by seventeen numbered chapters. No chapter headings are given beyond their Roman numerals, from Chapter I through Chapter XVII. Nothing else about setting, people, or plot appears on the page shown here.
self-control-a-novel:
Mary Brunton published this novel in 1811 and inscribed it, with warm praise, to the playwright Joanna Baillie. Brunton calls herself a person marked for obscurity, unknown to the world as a writer. She claims one point of kinship with Baillie: purity of intent in her work.

A motto from Cowper sets the theme: a man's true warfare lies within himself. The tale tests its people against passion and impulse, urging rule of the self as the path to honor. Readers meet an early nineteenth-century moral novel that treats feeling as a force to be governed, not obeyed.
shavings-a-novel:
Joseph C. Lincoln wrote this Cape Cod novel around the town of Orham and its champion talker, Gabriel Bearse. Chapter one finds Gabriel strangely silent yet plainly happy as he hurries down the main road. Captain Sam Hunniwell's old rule held that Gabriel was happy only when talking, and Orham agreed.

The flaw in that rule proves small: Gabriel has just gained a choice piece of news. He savors the talk it will fuel across town, volley after volley. Lincoln builds a warm comic world of gossips, sea captains, and small-town pride, where a shaving of news can reshape a whole day.
sir-mortimer-a-novel:
Mary Johnston published this novel in 1904, after To Have and To Hold had made her name. A list of pictures sets the tone: Sir John thrusting himself between two men, Baldry's little ship the Star, and Damaris hearing her hero called traitor. A friar's blank face under questions closes the list.

Chapter one opens on Mortimer's farewell speech, weighing what befalls if the sea claims the adventurers. Bones on strange shores and a queen's white touch consecrating unworthy men fill his words. Johnston builds a tale of honor, love, and suspected treason in the age of sea adventure.
sir-nigel:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote this tale of a young squire in the age of Edward the Third. Contents open with the house of Loring and the devil's coming to Waverley. Nigel stands trial before the abbot, holds the bridge at Tilford, and hawks with the king on Crooksbury Heath.

Later chapters cross to Calais, Spain's ships at sea, and the famed fight of thirty against thirty near Ploermel. Messengers ride to Cosford between deeds. Doyle packs the book with heraldry, courtesy, and hard fighting, in honor of the chivalry he loved to picture for modern boys and men.
sleeping-fires-a-novel:
Gertrude Atherton sets her novel Sleeping Fires in the San Francisco of the eighteen-sixties. No Burlingame yet stands, and the Western Addition is still a waste of sand dunes where goats roam the rocky gulches of Nob Hill. South of Market Street, by contrast, Rincon Hill and South Park form a calm home quarter, cold and aloof from the hot heart of the city.

Atherton walks the reader down Howard, Folsom, and Harrison Streets in detail. Large, plain houses, some shipped round the Horn, stand behind deep gardens with willows, oaks, statues, and fountains that sometimes run dry. High-walled gardens on Rincon Hill keep Castilian roses, a last trace of the Spain that ruled California before the gold-seekers came.
snake-and-sword-a-novel:
Percival Christopher Wren gave his novel Snake and Sword to his wife, Alice Lucille Wren. The contents divide the book into three parts named for a soul: its welding, its searing, and its saving. Chapter heads set a snake and a sword against each other again and again, with a woman named Lucille between them. Troopers of the Queen and a snake that pays back a haddock also figure in the list.

Part One opens with Colonel Matthew Devon de Warrenne of the Queen's Own Bombay Lancers. Grief-mad, he pins his Victoria Cross to the night-dress of his dying wife. The act, the narrator says, owns that she was the braver of the two. From that stark first scene, the snake and sword heads promise a fight worked out over years, with an epilogue set seven years on.
st-george-and-st-michael: George MacDonald wrote St. George and St. Michael in three volumes, printed at London in 1876. The opening pages give the contents of Volume I and the start of Volume II's list. Volume I opens with Dorothy and Richard, then Richard and his father, the witch, and a chapter of fools. Heads on preparations, an adventure, love and war, and Dorothy's refuge follow, with Raglan Castle, the two marquises, and a magician's vault in the mix.
strangers-at-lisconnel:
Jane Barlow's Strangers at Lisconnel, printed at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1895, is subtitled A Second Series of Irish Idylls. Barlow returns to the same poor western Irish village world as her earlier idylls, with chapter tales instead of one long plot.

The opening chapters are Out of the Way, Jerry Dunne's Basket, and Mrs. Kilfoyle's Cloak. A Gaelic line stands under the dedication, and the talk and manners are those of a remote place where a stranger's arrival is an event. Barlow writes with close sympathy for tenants and laborers, letting small incidents of baskets, cloaks, and visits carry the weight of village life.
success-a-novel:
Samuel Hopkins Adams, author of The Clarion and Common Cause, published the novel Success in 1921. Its three parts carry plain, fateful titles: Enchantment, The Vision, and Fulfillment, promising the rise of a man measured against the thing he chased.

The book opens at Manzanita. The lonely desert station stands sharp in keen February sunlight. The town lies a mile away in a dip of cactus country. It is a sorry sprawl of frame buildings. Rare rains have set the desert blooming, from scarlet ocatilla to pale yucca, while storm clouds mass in the southwest. Adams sets ambition in a hard, bright landscape where a railroad line runs as uncompromising as the engineers' mathematics.
sword-and-gown-a-novel:
Sword and Gown, a novel by the author of Guy Livingstone, was printed at New York in 1859; a transcriber's note names the author as George Alfred Lawrence. The sword and the gown of the title point to the two callings, soldier and clergyman, between which its hero's world turns.

The tale opens on a December shore below the maritime Alps, where Harry Molyneux lies in the sun and thanks the sea breeze aloud. His cheek is pale but for one round scarlet spot where consumption had hung out her flag of no surrender months before. Fir woods and stone pines stand sentinel above the coast. Lawrence, a muscular writer of military tales, sets a dying officer's rest cure against the pull of action and love.
sylvia-s-marriage-a-novel:
Upton Sinclair's Sylvia's Marriage, a novel printed at London, is the sequel to his Sylvia, and the press notices at its front state its theme without flinching. T.P.'s Weekly calls it a novel frankly devoted to showing the dangers that society runs through the marriage of unsound men with unsuspecting women.

The Times grants a large point. No reader ignorant of the ravages of the evil could refuse agreement with Sinclair. The Nation calls the book very severe and courageous. It calls the indictment appalling in its truth. The contents divide Sylvia's course into three books: Sylvia as Wife, Sylvia as Mother, and Sylvia as Rebel. Sinclair, the author of The Jungle, again turns fiction into a public health brief, this time on venereal disease and the double standard.
tanakh-jps-1917-daniel:
Daniel is a book of the Hebrew Bible given here in the 1917 English rendering of the Jewish Publication Society, made from the Masoretic Text. Its first chapter is set in exile, after Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon has besieged Jerusalem and seized goods from God's house.

The king orders bright youths of Israel to learn the tongue and lore of the Chaldeans at his court. Among them stand Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who gain new Babylonian names. Daniel then resolves in his heart not to stain himself with the king's rich food and wine. Readers follow faith held firm inside a foreign court, where court tales and visions test that faith.
tanakh-jps-1917-ezekiel:
Ezekiel is a long prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the English of the Jewish Publication Society dated 1917. Ezekiel is named as a priest, son of Buzi, living among the captives by the river Chebar in the land of the Chaldeans.

In the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's exile, the heavens open above him in a storm of fire and bright light. Four living beings come out of the cloud, each with four faces and four wings, their feet like burnished brass. Readers meet some of the Bible's most strange and vivid visions, joined to sharp words on guilt, loss, and a hoped-for return from exile.
tanakh-jps-1917-i-samuel:
First Samuel is a narrative book of the Hebrew Bible, given here in the Jewish Publication Society translation dated 1917. It begins not with a king but with a household in the hill country of Ephraim, headed by Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim.

Elkanah has two wives, Peninnah with children and Hannah with none, and each year he goes up to worship at Shiloh. Hannah, mocked by her rival, weeps and will not eat, though her husband gives her a double share. In deep grief she prays by the temple door where Eli the priest sits. Readers meet the birth tale of Samuel, and with it the shift from judges toward kings in Israel.
tanakh-jps-1917-ii-samuel:
Second Samuel is a narrative book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society's English rendering of 1917. It picks up David's story at a grim turn, just after the death of Saul in battle.

David has come back to Ziklag from a fight with the Amalekites when a man arrives with torn clothes and dust on his head. He reports that Israel fled the field and that Saul and Jonathan are both dead. He claims Saul begged him for a death blow on Mount Gilboa, and that he obeyed. Readers enter David's rise to full kingship, a reign of wins, grief, and grave faults told with rare depth.
tanakh-jps-1917-joel:
Joel is a short prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society rendering dated 1917. The book names its speaker as Joel son of Pethuel and gives no kings or dates to place him.

Joel calls the old men and all who live in the land to hear and pass the word down. He asks if such a thing has been seen in their days or in the days of their fathers. What follows is a plague of locusts read as a sign of God's great day. Readers get brief, vivid verse that moves from stripped fields and mourning to a call for fasting, prayer, and hope of rich rains restored.
the-american-baron-a-novel: Only title and publisher's pages are present for The American Baron, a novel by James De Mille printed by Harper and Brothers of New York in 1872. De Mille is billed as author of The Dodge Club, The Cryptogram, and Cord and Creese, each priced on the facing list in paper and cloth. A frontispiece caption shows clergymen slowly coming out of a house as others stand by, credited to page 132 of the pictured edition.
the-art-of-travel: A contents list lays out Francis Galton's The Art of Travel. It was first published in Great Britain by John Murray of London in 1872. Galton calls it a store of shifts and contrivances for wild countries. Heads run from first enquiries and fitting out an expedition through medicine, surveying tools, log-books, climbing, cattle, swimming, rafts, fords, clothing, bedding, tents, fire, food, and water. Later parts treat guns, game, fishing, signals, finding the way, caches, and dealings with the people of the country, ending with mechanical helps.
the-bad-man-a-novel:
Charles Hanson Towne turned Porter Emerson Browne's play into a novel, published by Putnam in 1921. A picture shows Holbrook Blinn in the title role, and the book is dedicated to him. Chapter headings use an old style, spelling out what each chapter will show.

The first heading tells of a young American who comes to a new country, meets hard luck, and draws a neighbour's eye to his ranch. A second man hears of wealth along the border and travels down to see it. Uncle Henry speaks his mind, a man called Red shows his heart, and Mrs Quinn gives coffee and advice.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-10-2-s:
Second Samuel in King James wording, begins after Saul's death, with David returned from fighting the Amalekites. David stays two days in Ziklag. Verses carry a triple number for book, chapter, and verse, a plain aid for finding each line.

On the third day a man comes from Saul's camp with torn clothes and earth on his head. He bows before David and reports that the people fled, many fell, and Saul and Jonathan are dead. Asked how he knows, he tells of finding Saul leaning on his spear on Mount Gilboa. News, grief, and a claim that will be tested open the book.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-26-eze:
Ezekiel in King James translation, starts in a thirtieth year, in the fourth month, as the prophet sits among captives by the river Chebar. Heavens open and he sees visions of God.

The date is tied to the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity. The word comes expressly to Ezekiel the priest, son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans, and God's hand is on him. A whirlwind comes from the north, a great cloud with fire and brightness like amber. From it comes the likeness of four living creatures, each with a human form and four faces.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-27-dan:
Daniel , from the King James Bible, opens in the third year of Jehoiakim, when Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieges Jerusalem. God gives the king into his hand, along with part of the temple vessels, carried to the land of Shinar.

The Babylonian king orders Ashpenaz to bring select children of Israel, of royal and princely seed. They must be without blemish, well favoured, skilful in wisdom, and able to stand in the palace. They are to be taught the learning and tongue of the Chaldeans, with daily food from the king's meat and wine. Exile and court training begin together.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-9-1-sa:
First Samuel in the authorised King James wording, opens with a man of Ramathaimzophim, on Mount Ephraim, named Elkanah. His line is given through Jeroham, Elihu, Tohu, and Zuph, an Ephrathite.

Elkanah had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none. Each year he went up to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh, where Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas were priests. At the offering he gave portions to Peninnah and her children, but a worthy portion to Hannah, whom he loved, though the Lord had shut her womb. Her rival provoked her.
the-boy-allies-at-lie-ge-or-through-line:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies at Liège, or Through Lines of Steel, dated 1915. The first chapter is called The Two Comrades. It opens in a great hotel in Berlin, where Hal Paine dashes through a packed lobby to his mother's side. His friend Chester Crawford runs at his heels.

Hal shouts that war has been declared, and that the Kaiser has made war on France. Mrs. Paine rises, grips her chair, and turns pale. She asks if men will once more fly at each other's throats, and if Europe will once more be a field of war. Hal drops to his knees and swears no one will harm an American. His mother smiles faintly and says her fear is not for herself. She thinks of old days, and of the wives and mothers whose hearts the news will tear.
the-cathedral-a-novel: Hugh Walpole, author of Jeremy and The Secret City, wrote this novel, dedicated to Jessie and Joseph Conrad. Only the dedication and contents are present here. They divide the book into three parts named Prelude, The Whispering Gallery, and The Jubilee, with chapters about the Brandons, the Ronders, Joan, and Falk.The work's own pages are not present here.
the-christmas-angel: Abbie Farwell Brown wrote this Christmas tale for children, with pictures. Only a publisher's list of her other books and the start of the title page are present here. The list names John of the Woods, The Book of Saints and Friendly Beasts, and The Curious Book of Birds. Prices are given, from Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York. A picture caption reads: You hang it on the tree, Angelina.Only the frame of the book is present, not its pages.
the-colossus-a-novel: Opie Read, author of The Jucklins and A Kentucky Colonel, wrote this novel, published at Chicago by Laird and Lee in 1893. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The chapters open with early life recalled, a sleepy village and a fussy old man, darkness, and a strange request. Later titles name the domain of a great merchant, interviewers, and acknowledgment by society.The story, if any, begins beyond what is present.
the-coryston-family-a-novel: Mrs. Humphry Ward's novel The Coryston Family was published in 1913 with pictures by Elizabeth Shippen Green. The list of illustrations hints at the cast. Marcia sings as she comes in. A son studies his mother's strong, lined face. An orator rises to his closing words while talk drops around him. Book I is headed Lady Coryston and opens under a Greek motto. Only the title pages, the picture list, and the head of Book I are present here, so the story itself does not appear.
the-crock-of-gold-a-rural-novel:
Martin Farquhar Tupper, author of Proverbial Philosophy, wrote The Crock of Gold as a rural novel, printed at Hartford by Silas Andrus and Son in 1851. Chapter I, The Labourer and His Dawning Discontent, opens at five on a raw March morning. Roger Acton rises from his poor pallet in the dark and cold, since his work lies two miles off and Master Jennings shows no favor to late men.

Honest Roger, called Steady Acton, is the best hand in the parish. Tupper presents him as a fair specimen of the English laboring class: just, hard-working, and patient, loyal to altar and throne, yet ground down by low wages. Such men fill barns to bursting for others, he writes, while their own children cry for bread.
the-dead-secret-a-novel: Wilkie Collins's The Dead Secret, first dated 1856, appears here in the New York illustrated edition from Harper and Brothers, dated 1874. A frontispiece line quotes Andrew Treverton announcing his own name. The title page names Collins as author of The Woman in White, Poor Miss Finch, No Name, Man and Wife, and The Moonstone. A publisher's list of his novels in Harper's Illustrated Library Edition follows, at a dollar fifty a volume. Only the front matter and that list are present here.
the-doctor-s-wife-a-novel:
The Doctor's Wife, a novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret and Aurora Floyd, was printed in London by John and Robert Maxwell. Its contents open with a young man from the country, then a sensation author, then Isabel. George Gilbert's holiday ends, George goes home, and a chapter called Too Much Alone hints at a wife left lone too long.

Mary Elizabeth Braddon's tale reworks a famed French plot of boredom and desire in an English key. Isabel reads cheap novels and dreams past her dull marriage. The chapter list promises bridges, birthdays, and slow ruin.
the-elusive-pimpernel:
Baroness Orczy's The Elusive Pimpernel opens in Paris in 1793, amid a wild surge of anarchy that shows no ebb. Its contents then step back: a retrospect, ex-ambassador Chauvelin, a Richmond gala, and Sir Percy and his lady. Later heads name a challenge, a passport, Boulogne, and the hostage.

Sir Percy Blakeney, the Scarlet Pimpernel, risks his life to snatch French nobles from the guillotine. His wife Marguerite stands at the plot's heart. Orczy mixes love, spies, and last-minute saves in her most famed vein. The Terror's shadow hangs over London's balls.
the-english-novel:
George Saintsbury's The English Novel, printed at London in 1913, surveys the form in eight chapters. They run from the foundation in romance. Then comes Lyly to Swift, and the four wheels of the novel wain. Scott and Miss Austen follow. The road runs on to Thackeray, the mid-Victorian novel, and the fiction of yesterday. Saintsbury, professor at Edinburgh, opens with a puzzle: prose fiction came late.

Greece and Rome, he notes, left next to no true novels till late days. His brisk, opinion-rich tour names the great and the minor alike. Few guides cover so much ground with such verve.
the-fashionable-adventures-of-joshua-cra:
David Graham Phillips wrote The Fashionable Adventures of Joshua Craig, a novel of Washington life and high society. The contents trace Craig from his first dressing for a grand house to a last chapter that names a Mrs. Joshua Craig.

The tale opens in a top-floor flat of the Wyandotte, the city's most costly apartment hotel. Craig steps into the best society, meets a desperate young woman, and stirs fights, confessions, and a belated proposal. Madam Bowker gives or withholds her blessing as Craig claws his way up. Phillips shows a raw climber at work among the rich and well born.
the-fifth-wheel-a-novel: Olive Higgins Prouty wrote The Fifth Wheel as a novel, printed at New York in 1916 with four pictures by James Montgomery Flagg. Only the front matter is present here, plus one line of speech under the front picture, where a woman tells Breck she would not marry him for anything in the world. Prouty, author of Bobbie, General Manager, gives the book to her mother. No chapter text appears in these opening pages.
the-financier-a-novel: Theodore Dreiser wrote The Financier as a novel, and only the front matter and contents are present here. The contents list runs to at least forty-one chapters, each named by number alone with no heads or hints of scene. No page of the story itself follows in the pages given here, so nothing about its hero or his deals can be told from these opening pages alone.
the-fortunes-of-nigel:
Sir Walter Scott wrote The Fortunes of Nigel as a novel of London in the days of King James, and his introduction explains his choice of hero. The hero's model is George Heriot, the king's goldsmith.

Scott tells how Heriot, a rich Edinburgh craftsman, followed James south, died in 1624 with no children, and left his wealth to found a school. Heriot's Hospital still raised and taught one hundred and thirty boys a year in Scott's day. On that plain, good man Scott builds Nigel, a young Scot lord in London who must keep his honor amid a sly court and a wild city.
the-forty-niners-a-chronicle-of-the-cali:
Stewart Edward White wrote The Forty-Niners as a tale of the California gold rush and the road west, printed in 1918. Sixteen chapters run from Spanish days to the triumph of the vigilantes.

White starts with the old order: native folk, Spanish soldiers, monks, and sleepy ranch life. Gold breaks that calm. Chapters cross the plains, pass the Mormons, and sail by Panama to the diggings. San Francisco burns, grows wild, and twice hangs its rogues by mob law. White, who knew the West first hand, shows how fast a land can change when gold calls the world to its hills.
the-grain-of-dust-a-novel:
David Graham Phillips wrote The Grain of Dust. It is a novel, dated 1911. Pictures are by A. B. Wenzell. Chapter I opens in a New York law office. The firm is Lockyer, Sanders, Benchley, Lockyer and Norman, corporation lawyers. Radical speakers call the firm infamous. It is among the most important firms in the city.

Into those offices on a December afternoon drifts a girl. She seeks work at stenography and typewriting. She seems as small and obscure an atom as the city hides. She is blonde, tawny-haired, fair-skinned, and blue-eyed. At a glance there is nothing definite about her. The contrast is the book's engine. A grain of dust of a girl is set down in a great law firm. The picture captions promise love, pride, and death ahead.
the-grand-babylon-ho-tel: Arnold Bennett wrote The Grand Babylon Hotel. Its subtitle names T. Racksole and Daughter. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty chapters. The heads open with The Millionaire and the Waiter. They name How Mr. Racksole Obtained His Dinner. They name an entrance of the Prince, and Nella and the Prince. They name two women and a revolver, a court pawnbroker, and Rocco and Room No. 111. They end with Royalty at the Grand Babylon. No chapter text is present.
the-great-god-success-a-novel: John Graham wrote The Great God Success. The name is a pen name of David Graham Phillips. The Gregg Press of Ridgewood, New Jersey, printed the book. Only front matter is present here: the title page and a contents list. The heads run from The Candidate from Yale and The City Editor Reconsiders through A Park Row Celebrity. Later heads name Yellow Journalism and The News-Record Gets a New Editor. The list points to a tale of a young newspaper man's rise. No chapter text is present.
the-guardian-angel:
Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote The Guardian Angel. His preface, addressed to his readers, explains the tale. It forms a natural sequence to his former story, Elsie Venner.
