That tale rested on an experiment: an alien element in a child's blood before birth, giving ophidian traits. It raised the limits of human responsibility. This story comes nearer common experience. It traces inherited traits in body and mind.

Holmes tells a story from Jonathan Edwards the younger. A brutal man in New Haven was dragging his father along the ground. The old man cried out: do not drag me further, for I did not drag my father beyond this tree. Holmes has tried to show the evolution of inherited qualities in Myrtle Hazard. He shows them plainly, but not so much as to disturb the narrative.
the-haunted-chamber-a-novel:
The Haunted Chamber is a novel by The Duchess, dated 1888. Chapter one opens at dusk around an old castle, where twilight lies on flowers, fountains, and ivy-covered walls. High in the old tower sits the chamber of the title, a room no servant of the castle will enter, wrapped in gloom and old legend.

Stories told about the room give it a grim past. A Stuart-era earl is said to have hanged himself there rather than face dishonor. A fair lady was shut in the room and starved by her lord, and two men later fought a secret duel there that ended in both deaths. Blood stains on the boards are said to remain as proof.
the-haunting-of-low-fennel: Sax Rohmer wrote The Haunting of Low Fennel. The record is dated 1920. A contents list names three pieces in order. The title story runs in six numbered parts. The Valley of the Just follows, in seven parts. It is described as a story of the Shan Hills. The Blue Monkey comes third, in at least three parts. Only the contents list is present here. The stories themselves do not appear.
the-heart-of-rachael:
Kathleen Norris wrote The Heart of Rachael, shown as Volume VI of her works. Chapter one opens on a bright April Saturday at the Long Island Country Club at Belvedere Bay. Two hundred players spread over the golf links, men in plaid stockings and striped sweaters, women in scarlet coats and white skirts against the fresh green grass.

Norris fills the scene with seasonal change. Lilac and early roses scent the air, motor cars run on the roadway, riders use the bridle path, and crowds wait at the first tee. Mrs. Archibald Buckney is introduced among the watchers at the last green. Golf rules the day, and summer feels real again after winter.
the-heritage-of-the-desert-a-novel: Zane Grey wrote The Heritage of the Desert. The title page labels it a novel. The contents list twenty-one chapters. The names lean hard on the desert. Early titles include The Sign of the Sunset and White Sage. Later titles include The Trail of the Red Wall and The Oasis. Silvermane, Echo Cliffs, and Thunder River also appear. The list ends with Mescal. The record present here holds front matter only. The heading of chapter one also appears. The novel itself does not appear.
the-italians-a-novel: Frances Elliot published this novel in 1875, dedicating it to the real Enrica with the author's love. Her Diary of an Idle Woman in Italy was hers too. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The contents build the tale around Lucca. Its cathedral and three witches open part one. The Marchesa Guinigi at home follows. Count Marescotti and a countess's ball appear. Part two brings calumny and the Guinigi tower. Enrica's trial and its outcome close that part.
the-lady-s-album-of-fancy-work-for-1850-:
The publishers of this album for 1850 offer fancy-work designs. Knitting, netting, crochet, braiding, and embroidery fill it. Clear directions for working the patterns come with them. Their address to readers recalls former efforts' kind welcome. That welcome encouraged this similar production. No expense was spared on pictures or letterpress. An elegant ornament for the drawing-room was the aim. A useful ally at the work-table was the second aim. Every recent style appears, with nothing in fashion omitted.

An opening essay gives the needle an ancient dignity. Embroidery is ascribed to the Phrygians. Sidonian excellence follows in the account. Robes of gold and silver came after the Norman Conquest. The Bayeux Tapestry stands as Queen Matilda's lasting trophy. Knitting, by contrast, arrived in the mid-sixteenth century. Spaniards and Scots dispute its invention. A pair of knitted hose was once a fit present between sovereigns.
the-league-of-the-scarlet-pimpernel:
Baroness Orczy opens a linked set of Scarlet Pimpernel tales in revolutionary Paris. A young woman dances in a lanthorn lit street circle, striking a beribboned tambourine with a grimy hand. Starvation and daily cruelty have hardened her mouth and sunk her eyes.

Crowds gather, watch, and melt away when she begs for alms. Tumbrils carrying aristocrats to the guillotine form the usual street spectacle of these days. Sir Percy Blakeney league works inside that terror, rescuing victims through disguise, forged papers, and bold tricks played under the noses of guards.
the-lever-a-novel:
William Dana Orcutt published his Washington novel in 1911 under an Archimedes motto about a lever long enough to move the world. Chapter one rides along a maple lined road from Washington toward Chevy Chase. A girl in a slow carriage looks back at a young man in a passing automobile.

Alice Gorham flushes at his gaze, then wonders if he could be Allen Sanford, a Pittsburgh childhood playmate unseen since her mother died. Her aunt and her ten year old sister Patricia tease the moment open. Orcutt sets a society romance inside capital politics and new wealth.
the-life-story-of-an-old-rebel: John Denvir published his life story in Dublin in 1910, after writing The Irish in Britain and other works. Only the title page and contents are present here. Chapters run from early recollections and coming over from Ireland to O Connell in Liverpool. The Great Famine, the Irish Revolutionary Brotherhood, and the rising of 1867 follow in the list. Later chapters promise the Manchester rescue, Michael Davitt penal servitude, and the Home Rule movement. The memoir itself stays beyond the pages held in this record.
the-little-colonel:
Annie Fellows Johnston published The Little Colonel in 1895, dedicating it to a Kentucky girl described as the heroine herself. The story opens at the gate of a fine old Kentucky estate called Locust. A small girl in a temper reaches up on tiptoes at the iron bars, a Scotch terrier beside her, looking down a long avenue of locust trees toward a white-pillared stone house.

Behind the vines on the porch sits the old Colonel, whom she cannot see. Illustration captions stress that the same temper burns in the child's eyes as in his, and that she answers, "'Cause I'm so much like you." Readers meet a spirited granddaughter whose likeness to her grandfather drives the story of their meeting.
the-littlest-rebel:
Edward Peple's The Littlest Rebel carries a 1914 copyright and was published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Chapter one introduces young Mrs. Herbert Cary, who sits under the trees with her work basket, trying to plan a dress for her daughter out of odds and ends of nothing. Her daughter Virgie, a tot of seven with sun-touched hair and dark eyes, comes running with her beloved doll, Susan Jemima, clutched to her breast.

Behind Virgie comes her playmate Sally Ann, barefoot in a tattered gingham dress, carrying a pointed stick like a sword. The opening sets a household short of money and material, with a lively small girl at its center. Peple builds the scene on contrast: a mother's worry over scraps, and children turning sticks and moss into play.
the-living-link-a-novel:
James De Mille, author of The Dodge Club and The Cryptogram, wrote The Living Link, a novel whose first chapter is headed A Terrible Secret. On a May evening in 1840, the girls of Plympton Terrace, a fashionable boarding-school by Derwentwater, gather on the portico in a strange hush. They walk arm in arm and talk in low, earnest tones over one engrossing subject, all oppressed by a common sadness.

A galloping horse breaks the quiet. A girl of about eighteen rides in at full speed, leaps down, and sends the horse off to its stall. She is dark and striking, with deep hazel eyes full of energetic life, yet an earnestness deepening toward melancholy hints that sorrow has already marked her young life.
the-maid-at-arms-a-novel: Robert W. Chambers wrote The Maid-at-Arms, dated 1902 with illustrations by Howard Chandler Christy. Only the title page, contents, and list of illustrations are present, so the novel itself does not appear. The twenty-two chapters run from The Road to Varicks' and Sir Lupus through A Night at the Patroon's, The Ghost-Ring, The False-Faces, and Oriskany, to The End of the Beginning. Captions name George Ormond and show Jack Mount looming colossal in beaded buckskins, pointing to a Revolutionary-era border tale.
the-merchant-of-berlin-an-historical-nov: L. Mühlbach's historical novel The Merchant of Berlin, translated from the German by Amory Coffin. Only its title page and the contents of Book I appear here, dated 1910, so the novel itself does not appear. The chapter titles open with a festival and a workman's holiday, then promise the Russian at the gates, a night of horrors, and Russians and Austrians. Later headings turn to a maiden's heart, a faithful friend, a fugitive, and an eavesdropper.
the-midnight-passenger-a-novel: Richard Henry Savage's novel The Midnight Passenger shows only its contents and the heading of its first chapter here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents divide the book into three parts: Under the Arch, An Inside Ring, and The Message from Amoy. Chapter titles promise a Danube picture, shadows of the Brooklyn Bridge, and a strange tug's voyage. Later chapters name a girl bride's rebellion, a lonely pursuer, and a Miss Worthington sharing her secret.
the-morals-of-marcus-ordeyne-a-novel:
William J. Locke's novel The Morals of Marcus Ordeyne is narrated by Ordeyne himself, writing in Verona from his open diary. Part I, Chapter I reaches back six months to a happy afternoon in May. The entry for May 20th marks the seventh anniversary of his release from captivity, meaning his escape from schoolmastering.

For seven years he has been free of Jones Minor and Euclid's First Book, he writes with thanksgiving. Born schoolmasters may enjoy boys; he became only an automaton, feared by himself and teased by colleagues. Seven years earlier a lawyer's letter reached him just before first school, in his classroom. Its news of wholesale destruction among his relatives left him ghastly-faced before thirty silent boys, and one pupil loudly guessed he had got the sack.
the-morgesons-a-novel:
Elizabeth Stoddard's novel The Morgesons, in a 1901 printing with her portrait from a daguerreotype, carries a long preface about how a non-literary girl became a novelist. Stoddard supposes environment caused her writing. Leaving her native village, she never dreamed imagination would lead her back, since village annals did not interest her and she was not studious.

Her tribe knew nothing of literature, she writes; reading was merely for amusement and was held against her as an unprofitable fault. Moral works or endless white sewing were thought fitter uses of her time. She cared for heroes, not authors, admiring Miss Porter's Sobieski and Bulwer's Ernest Maltravers. Only after living among book-makers, poor and married to a poet in a garret, did idle hours and wounded pride push her to write.
the-nest-builder-a-novel:
Beatrice Forbes-Robertson Hale's novel The Nest-Builder, with a frontispiece by J. Henry, is built in five parts whose titles follow a bird's progress: Mate-Song, Mated, The Nestling, Wings, and The Builder. Hale is billed as author of What Women Want. Part I, Mate-Song, opens at sea aboard the Lusitania.

Outbound from Liverpool, the great liner bucks down the Irish Sea through a September gale. In the second-class quarters aft, every shouldering wave brings a sickening vibration as one of the ship's propellers races clear of the water. The gong has sounded for the second sitting at dinner. Trails of hungry, weary travellers troop down the companionway, meeting files of still more uneasy diners coming up from the first.
the-precipice-a-novel:
Elia W. Peattie's novel The Precipice was published by Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1914. It shares its title with Goncharov's novel in a neighbouring record, but the two books are unrelated. An epigraph speaks of a fanfare of trumpets that women the world over are listening to, stirred even against their wills. That call hangs over the story as a new force in women's lives.

Chapter I finds Kate Barrington with her degree and graduating honours behind her. The banquets, breakfasts, and farewell gatherings are through, and she is going home. The Chicago spring has drawn to a close so slowly that the campus still looks poorly equipped for summer. Kate tells her friend Lena Vroom, who sees her off at the station, how much further things will be advanced down-state. She plans to cut roses first thing for the Dresden vases at home.
the-president-a-novel: Alfred Henry Lewis's novel The President was published at New York by A. S. Barnes and Company in 1904. Lewis is named as author of The Boss and Wolfville Days, and the book is inscribed to Ethel Oviatt Lewis. The pages shown give the title matter and first contents entries. Chapter titles repeat a pattern: How Richard Began to Woo, How a President is Bred, and How Mr. Gwynn Dined with the Harleys. Later entries promise a speakership fought for and Storri plotting vengeance. The story itself is not shown.
the-queen-of-sheba-and-my-cousin-the-col:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich pairs two long stories in a 1907 Boston and New York volume of his writings. The first follows Edward Lynde, assistant cashier at the Nautilus Bank in Rivermouth, who in June 1872 can finally carry out a long-planned secret scheme.

Chapters move through a family quarrel, travels beyond the sea, the Denhams, and Alpine scenes between Geneva and Chamouni under Mont Blanc. The companion piece concerns a colonel honored for bravery in battle. Readers get Aldrich's polished New England storytelling joined to European travel and gentle social comedy.
the-quest-of-the-silver-fleece-a-novel:
W. E. B. Du Bois published his novel of cotton and race in the American South in 1911 with A. C. McClurg and Company. Contents move from dreams and a school through Miss Mary Taylor, a town, a girl named Zora, and the planting and flowering of cotton.

Later headings bring Harry Cresswell, a dinner at Mrs. Grey's, love, revelation, and a great refusal. The silver fleece is cotton itself, tied to schooling, land, and ambition under Jim Crow. Readers get a serious literary treatment of Black life and the cotton economy from a major American thinker writing fiction.
the-ramrodders-a-novel:
Holman Day wrote King Spruce before this political novel of 1910. Contents open with the baiting of an ancient lion. A line-up of the fight follows. Caucuses appear twice in the headings. One shows a caucus as it was planned. The other shows how it was run. A household visit and a state web of deals come between.

Later headings promise a political convert. A man steps out of the shadows. A double campaign unfolds. Hands are dealt like cards at the close. Only the title pages and contents list are present here. The campaign narrative itself does not appear on these pages.
the-scarlet-pimpernel:
Baroness Orczy's The Scarlet Pimpernel opens in Paris in September 1792, according to its contents. Later chapters move to Dover and Richmond, then back to Calais. Marguerite, Lord Grenville's ball, and a scrap of paper figure in the headings. The league of the Scarlet Pimpernel is named early. An escape closes the list of thirty-one chapters.

Chapter one shows the West Barricade in Paris. A surging crowd waits there a little before sunset. Orczy calls them human only in name. To eye and ear they seem savage creatures, she writes. Vile passions animate them, along with lust for vengeance and hate. A decade later, she notes, a proud tyrant would raise a monument at that very spot.
the-sheik-a-novel:
E. M. Hull's novel The Sheik, dated 1921, opens at the Biskra Hotel. Lady Conway refuses to watch the dancing. She thoroughly disapproves of the expedition the dance inaugurates, she declares. Diana Mayo plans a tour alone into the desert, she protests. No chaperon or attendant of her own sex will go. Only native camel drivers and servants will attend her.

Such recklessness casts a slur on Diana's reputation and her country's prestige, Lady Conway insists. A companion answers that Miss Mayo's unusual upbringing should be remembered. Lady Conway interrupts that the upbringing was deplorable, but excuses nothing. She had expostulated with Diana and her brother Sir Aubrey in vain. She washes her hands of the affair, she says. Drawing her wrap around her, she stalks across the verandah.
the-soul-of-democracy-the-philosophy-of-:
Edward Howard Griggs published this philosophy of the World War in 1918, subtitled as a study of the war in relation to human liberty. Its motto sets man for the state, meaning autocracy and imperialism, against man for mankind, which Griggs calls the soul of democracy. Twenty-two chapters range from the conflict of ideas to preparedness, socialism, feminism, education, and moral leadership.

The opening chapter, The World Tragedy, calls the war the greatest disaster in human history, greater even than the fall of Rome. Griggs says the war came utterly unanticipated in its world extent, leaving people bewildered, and his chapters work through what democracy must become in response.
the-story-of-the-red-cross-as-told-to-th: Annie Fellows Johnston's story of the Red Cross, told to her Little Colonel, is presented here through a publisher's catalogue of her works alone. The catalogue lists the Little Colonel series volume by volume. Each book costs a dollar fifty. The Little Colonel stories lead off. The hero, Arizona, and Mary Ware volumes follow. A boxed set of twelve costs eighteen dollars. Doll books appear too. Illustrated holiday editions close the list. Johnston's Red Cross narrative itself does not appear.
the-tale-of-frisky-squirrel: Arthur Scott Bailey's Frisky Squirrel belongs to his Sleepy-Time Tales, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in 1915 with illustrations by Eleanore Fagan. Nothing beyond the front matter and chapter list survives in this record, so the story itself stays out of reach. Seventeen chapters are listed, following Frisky through a fall, a picnic, a visit to the gristmill, fun on the milldam, and a trapping inside an attic. Farmer Green's cat appears near the end, which hints at the danger waiting for a busy young squirrel.
the-three-black-pennys-a-novel: Joseph Hergesheimer's Three Black Pennys, copyrighted in 1917 by Alfred A. Knopf and reprinted by Grosset and Dunlap, is present here in front matter only. That matter includes a long verse-like dedication to John Hemphill, remembering June nights on the porch at Dower House, willow foliage powdered against stars, and candlelit dinners in April airs. A contents heading follows, but no chapter of the novel is shown. Readers receive Hergesheimer's lush dedication as a foretaste of his style, while the Pennys' story itself stays unread.
the-turmoil-a-novel:
Booth Tarkington's The Turmoil appeared in 1915, dedicated to Laurel. It opens in an unnamed midland city choked by the smoke of its own growth. A visitor feels the grime at once. The streets and air show a place that prizes money above cleanliness. Tarkington pictures the smoke as a giant's bad breath. The city pants for riches and fouls its own home. In its rush to get rich fast, it wastes real wealth.

A generation earlier the same place had been an easygoing big town of neighborly people, none very rich and few very poor, with clean air and time to live. Tarkington, who chronicled Indianapolis, builds his novel of the Sheridan family on that fall from homelike town to frantic city, a parable of industrial America.
the-twins-a-domestic-novel:
Martin Farquhar Tupper, author of Proverbial Philosophy, published The Twins, a domestic novel, at Hartford in 1851. Chapter one is headed Place, Time, Circumstance, and settles on Burleigh-Singleton, a pleasant little watering-place on England's southern coast. It suits people of small incomes and good consciences. The latter are indispensable. The town's cheapness in meat and drink is matched by its preeminent dullness in men and manners. Tupper then relents and enumerates its advantages.

The breezy Heights with a flag-staff get their praise. So do water-meadows along the dark Mullet river and Pacton Park. The market town of Eyemouth, the sea, and the picturesque mud-built village of Oxton complete the tour. Tupper's genial, rambling manner promises a comedy of small-town life, where twin heroes will stir a place that prides itself on being dull.
the-visioning-a-novel:
Susan Glaspell published her novel The Visioning in 1911 and opens it on a golf course. Miss Katherine Wayneworth Jones is bunkered, as she has been many times before, and she declines to take the situation tragically. The spring day is lazy, and she makes an arm-chair of her hazard instead.

Katie Jones is an army girl to the second and third generations, courted by bachelor officers and expected to marry inside the service. On her twenty-fifth birthday she considers matrimony with practical calm. Captain Harry Prescott will likely propose before summer ends, and she expects to accept. He plays good golf, dances well, and shows his teeth pleasingly when he laughs.
the-wharf-by-the-docks-a-novel:
Florence Warden published The Wharf by the Docks in 1896, and chapter one, Something Amiss, begins in Canterbury. The old city, she says, looks down contentedly on hurrying Americans photographing its cathedral and slums. Around it stand halls and mansions in Kentish valleys and on wooded hills, unknown to most visitors.

One such house, The Beeches, is a warm red-brick Jacobean place above a sleepy grazing landscape. George Wedmore, a London merchant, has bought back the former family home and retired there, though his family flippantly calls the move exile from Bayswater to a wilderness. After dinner the lean, fidgety Wedmore waits by the fire for Dr. Haselden, his chess partner.
the-wild-olive-a-novel:
The Wild Olive, published by Harper in 1910 and reprinted by Grosset and Dunlap with illustrations by Lucius Hitchcock, names its author only as the author of The Inner Shrine. An illustration caption warns that a hundred men are beating the mountain to find the fugitive. Part one is titled Ford, and chapter one drops that fugitive into an Adirondack wood-road at twilight.

He is tall, young, hatless, coatless, and barefoot, listening through wind in the pines for sounds his city-nurtured senses cannot sort. Four country constables escaped a few hours ago had fired shots after him. Every gust seems ready to burst with pursuers or weird armies of gnomes. None comes, and he speeds on through the leagues of forest.
the-workingman-s-paradise-an-australian-:
William Lane, writing as John Miller, published The Workingman's Paradise in 1892. He calls it an Australian labour novel. A contents list shows two parts with biblical titles. Part one follows Nellie showing Ned around Sydney. Chapters cover sweating in the slums and Saturday night in Paddy's Market. Socialism is named outright in one chapter title.

Part two moves toward Queensland and unemployment. Ned goes to his fate in the final chapter. The contents promise debates among poets, pressmen, and workers. Lane wrote to argue for labour's cause through fiction. Readers interested in early Australian socialism will find its program woven into a love story.
the-world-english-bible-web-1-samuel:
Book nine of the World English Bible, First Samuel, introduces Elkanah of Ramathaim Zophim. He lives in the hill country of Ephraim. Elkanah has two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. One wife has children, while Hannah has none. Each year the family travels to Shiloh to worship. Eli's sons serve there as priests.

At the sacrifice Elkanah gives Hannah a double portion. He loves her, though her womb is closed. Peninnah provokes her year after year until she weeps. Hannah refuses food in her grief. From this sorrow comes Samuel's birth story. Readers meet Israel on the edge of kingship, through one family's pain.
the-world-english-bible-web-2-samuel:
Book ten of the World English Bible, Second Samuel, opens after Saul's death. David has returned from defeating the Amalekites. He waits two days in Ziklag. On the third day a man arrives from Saul's camp. His clothes are torn and earth covers his head. He falls before David in respect.

David presses him for news of the battle. The man reports Israel fled and many fell. Saul and Jonathan, he says, are dead. David asks how he can be sure. The messenger's answer begins a tale David will test. Grief, kingship, and consequence drive the book that follows.
the-world-english-bible-web-daniel:
Daniel, book twenty-seven of the World English Bible, begins in besieged Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon comes in Jehoiakim's third year. Temple vessels are carried off to Shinar. The king orders choice Israelite youths brought to his court. They must be handsome, wise, and quick to learn. Chaldean language and learning will be taught to them.

Daily portions of royal food and wine are assigned. Daniel and his friends must decide how to live faithfully in exile. Courts, dreams, furnaces, and lions fill the chapters ahead. Readers get stories of loyalty under empire. Prophetic visions of kingdoms rising and falling complete the book.
the-world-english-bible-web-ezekiel:
Book twenty-six of the World English Bible gives Ezekiel's visions among Babylonian captives. Ezekiel sits by the river Chebar in the fifth year of exile. The heavens open, and God's hand rests on him. He is a priest, the son of Buzi. A stormy wind rolls in from the north. Lightning flashes around a great glowing cloud.

Four living creatures emerge from the fire's midst. Each has a human likeness, four faces, and four wings. Stranger visions follow: wheels, bones, and a measured temple. Ezekiel prophesies judgment, then restoration for Israel. Readers encounter the Bible's most vivid visionary writing. Exiles hear that God is not confined to Jerusalem.
three-men-on-the-bummel: Jerome K. Jerome's Three Men on the Bummel appears in a new edition from Arrowsmith at Bristol and London in 1914, illustrated by L. Raven Hill. Jerome dedicated the little work to good master Time. He calls Time a gentle guide, a laughter-loving philosopher, and a grave-faced jester. Time, he says, lets him go his own way yet brings him right, and teaches that even toothache will pass. The dedication pages are what is included in this record, so Jerome's German cycling tour itself does not appear here.
through-stained-glass-a-novel:
George Agnew Chamberlain, author of Home, published his novel with Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1915. Chapter one opens in 1866 at Rio de Janeiro, where the American minister watches Kentucky colonels wandering unfamiliar streets. His despatch to Secretary Seward warns of a vast Southern exodus to Brazil.

In fact few Confederate families came, and their small migration barely rippled the hemisphere. For those who suffered shipwreck, loss, and broken utopian dreams, Chamberlain calls it a tragedy of existence. Readers get a novel rooted in post-Civil War emigration and disappointed hopes of a free wilderness.
tommy-and-grizel: J. M. Barrie published Tommy and Grizel with illustrations by Bernard Partridge, in editions dated 1900 and 1912. A contents list for part one runs through fifteen chapters. Tommy finds a way, searches for treasure, and hears Sandys on woman in the opening headings. Grizel of the crooked smile arrives in chapter four, followed by the Tommy myth, ghosts in the den, and the beginning of a duel. A contents list alone is included in this record, so Barrie's novel itself is not shown.
tracy-park-a-novel:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes published her novel at Toronto with Rose Publishing in 1886, opening chapter one with a telegram. Arthur Tracey wires Frank Tracy at Tracy Park, Shannondale, from New York's Brevoort House on October sixth. He arrived that morning on the Scotia and will take the three o'clock train.

The clerk at Shannonville writes out and despatches the message to the Honourable Frank Tracy, lately elected to the state legislature. A Dickens motto about pressing forward instead of crying heads the chapter. Readers get a domestic novel launched by a homecoming announcement that will disturb a quiet town.
under-handicap-a-novel:
Jackson Gregory's Under Handicap, copyright 1914 by Harper and Brothers, is dedicated to his wife, Lotus McGlashan Gregory. A frontispiece shows Conniston finding a huddled heap almost at his feet. Chapter one crosses the desert by rail.

Outside the Overland Limited stretch shimmering heat and dry, thirsty sand in a gray, barren blur. Telegraph poles and two burning rails are all that mark man's passing through the vast waste. The train screams onward like a frightened thing, and the desert does not even return its echo. Gregory sets his western novel's scale at once: an immense, indifferent land against the small men crossing it.
undset-jenny-a-novel:
Jenny, in English translation, was the novel that first made Sigrid Undset's name before her medieval epics. Its heroine, Jenny Winge, is a young Norwegian painter working in Rome. She seeks both true art and true love, and finds the two hard to hold together.

A love affair that begins in hope turns sour and destructive. Jenny's pride, longing, and pride in her work pull her in opposed ways. Undset writes of women's inner lives with unusual frankness for her time. The book still feels modern in its pain, honesty, and refusal of easy comfort.
vain-fortune-a-novel:
George Moore asks his critics, in a prefatory note, to treat the 1895 new edition of Vain Fortune as a new book. He admits the first version was thin and dull, and says he rewrote it for an American printing, making Emily Watson the central figure in place of Hubert Price. Walter Scott of London issued this revised text, with five pictures by Maurice Greiffenhagen.

Moore then tells how the final form came about. A Dutch translator, Madam Couperus, compared the English and American versions and found good pages in each that the other lacked. She showed him the two could be joined without changing a sentence, an idea that had not struck him. Readers get a novel twice built, plus an author's frank account of why its first shape failed and how its heroine took the lead.
vellenaux-a-novel:
E. W. Forrest, author of The Blue Jacket and other tales, tried his hand as a novelist with Vellenaux in 1874. His preface tells readers that fact and fancy are so blended here that they will hardly tell where one ends and the other starts. Episodes rest on real service in India: the Sheik wars, the siege of Mooltan, the battle of Chillianwalla, and the Sepoy Mutiny, with names, dates, and places changed.

Forrest says the hero's adventures, escapes, and exploits were grafted from his own life and from those of many soldier friends, and he pledges that nothing has been overdrawn. Chapter one opens on an autumn day, with bright sun falling through stained glass into a room with curved, deep-set windows. Readers get an Anglo-Indian war novel built from a participant's store of real incidents, dressed as fiction.
we-can-t-have-everything-a-novel: Rupert Hughes wrote We Can't Have Everything, a novel with pictures by James Montgomery Flagg. Pages present here hold title pages, a list of Hughes's other books, and the contents, so the story itself is not shown. The contents divide the novel into four books, each named for a woman. Miss Kedzie Thropp comes to town in the first. Mrs. Tommie Gilfoyle has her picture taken in the second. Mrs. Jim Dyckman is not satisfied in the third, and the Marchioness has qualms in the fourth.
we-two-a-novel:
Edna Lyall wrote We Two, and her first chapter, Brian Falls in Love, opens with a small essay on place. People raised in the country, where every neighbor is known by sight, tend to think town life must lack the interests of their narrow circles. They watch the passing crowd of strangers. They wonder whether anyone could feel at home amid such change.

Londoners settled long in one quarter know better, Lyall says. Town life holds almost as many links between its actors as country life holds between its own. Silent greetings pass between passengers who share the same train each day. Omnibus conductors grow familiar. The organ-grinder's day and street are known in advance. Into that web of small London loyalties she sets Brian and his love, in a novel that joins private feeling to public causes.
when-egypt-went-broke-a-novel:
Holman Day wrote When Egypt Went Broke, a novel of a small town called Egypt. Chapter one shows Tasper Britt rising at gray dawn. Britt is the town money boss, nicknamed Twelve-per-cent Britt. Behind his back, debtors call him Pharaoh. Day compares him to fishermen who hunt worms at both ends of the day.

Nearly every man with property in Egypt owes Britt money. Debtors speak with care in his office, since each note renewal costs a bonus. Britt even dyed his beard and wears a scratch wig, sure of his standing. He took to dye after his wife Hittie died. Day builds a sharp tale of debt, pride, and a town in one man's grip.
wych-hazel: Susan Warner and Anna Warner wrote this novel, first issued in 1876. Pages present here hold review extracts and publisher's adverts, but no novel chapters. A long Atlantic Monthly review says the story tells Rollo's love for Wych Hazel. That review calls the dialogue crabbed and hard to follow. Friendlier notices from Boston papers promise fine fiction and lively talk instead. The clash of reviews is all these pages offer.
wyllard-s-weird-a-novel: M. E. Braddon published this three-volume novel in London in 1885. Pages present here hold the title page for volume one and the start of its chapter list. The first chapter is set in a Cornish valley. The second follows an inquest, and the third names a Joseph Distin. No chapter text itself appears in these pages. Braddon is billed as the author of Lady Audley's Secret and Vixen, which signals sensation fiction.
young-people-s-pride-a-novel: Stephen Vincent Benet published this novel in 1922, with pictures by Henry Raleigh. Pages present here hold the title page and a long dedication poem to Rosemary, but no novel chapters. In verse, Benet wishes he could steal Montmartre, Chartres glass, and gargoyles from Notre Dame for her. He offers only rhymes instead, calling them withered little things. A quoted note explains that young people's pride names a small flower blown about by winds.
zophiel: Mrs. Brooks wrote this poem, published in Boston in 1825 by Richardson and Lord. Pages present here hold the title page and a copyright deposit notice, but no poem text. The notice records the title deposited on August 12, 1825, in the Massachusetts district clerk's office. An Italian motto from Metastasio about fate growing tired of torment heads the title page. The poem's verses themselves do not appear in these pages.
